title: The Cooler
full_review:
In "The Cooler" (Lions Gate), sad sack William H. Macy plays Bernie, a guy so unlucky that his very presence at a Las Vegas casino table will immediately chill a winner's hot streak. In fact, that's his job at the Shangri-La Casino where after six years as a "cooler" he's almost finished paying off his gambling debt to his friend, Shelly (Alec Baldwin), the casino manager.

Lonely loser Bernie wants out to make a fresh start far from Vegas but Shelly needs him to stay. Enter casino cocktail waitress Natalie (Maria Bello) who shows unexpected interest in Bernie, so much so that she even takes him to bed. Bernie is startled, grateful and quickly moves beyond lust to love, which touches world-weary Natalie and evokes a genuine emotional response in her as well.

Meanwhile, Shelly is proving himself to be no friend in his determination to keep Bernie as an indentured servant. When one ploy begins to backfire, Shelly takes full advantage of catching Bernie's estranged son and pregnant wife (Shawn Hatosy and Estella Warren) trying to scam the casino. Brutally beating the son, Shelly orders the couple's deaths unless Bernie agrees to five more years at the casino, which of course he does.

But Shelly's manipulations are not finished. Bernie's self-esteem has returned thanks to Natalie's love, and his presence at a casino table no longer ruins a winning streak. In fact, people around him actually start getting lucky. Shelly decides to crush Bernie's love affair by physically abusing Natalie and from there the tale rushes towards its violent and not very credible conclusion.

Co-writer and director Wayne Kramer steeps the audience in a sleazy environment of gambling, promiscuity, violence and criminality in which few would want to linger. There is much to find objectionable in the film's use of language, brutality and graphic sexuality. Nonetheless, there is a raw honesty to the characterizations as each of the three leads experiences growth and inches toward redemption despite their considerable failings.

The sex scenes, while unnecessarily explicit, are not glamorized or titillating; on the contrary, they suggest a desperation for a connection to another human being, for a kind of sexual healing that in this story blossoms into transforming love.

What makes the film compelling is the trio of performances that anchor the action in the gritty reality of Vegas casinos. Bello's brittle-on-the-outside, wounded-within waitress strikes a chord, and Macy turns in another empathetic performance as a lovable loser who finds the courage to confront his faux friend. Reminiscent of his turn in "Glengarry Glen Ross," Baldwin channels his legendary temper into this role with a fury that is cringe-inducing. While Macy's Bernie is consistently the weakling nice guy, Shelly goes from somewhat sympathetic to mean to outright monster before beginning a wary turnaround.

The story explores themes of discouragement and hope, accountability and renewal and the possibility of healing love even in the most dire circumstances. In these aspects it is emotionally involving. However, it presupposes the audience will accept the notion of luck -- that Bernie can really cause people to win or lose at the gaming tables. That's a tall order, and the ending also strains audience credibility, leaving "The Cooler" a flawed if engrossing -- and very adult -- movie.

Because of a few intense sexual encounters with full nudity, some brutal violence, brief drug abuse, much rough language and intermittent profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
